segments.text: On the night of December fifth, in towns across the Alps, a shaggy figure with horns, a long red tongue, and rattling chains comes through the streets. His name is Krampus. He walks beside Saint Nicholas, the kind bishop who brings gifts, and he has come for the children who misbehaved. People often say that Krampus is far older than Christmas, an ancient pagan spirit of winter. But what do the oldest records actually show?

segments.text: The Krampus most people picture today owes a great deal to the postcard. In 1869, Austria-Hungary introduced what is often called the world's first official postcard. In the decades that followed, many colorful cards for the Nicholas season were printed, and Krampus appeared on many of them.

segments.text: On these cards, Krampus took a familiar shape: dark fur, horns, a long red tongue, chains, a bundle of twigs, and sometimes children carried off on his back. Some cards were meant to frighten. Others turned him into a striking piece of design. These cards, from a Vienna workshop around 1910, are now kept in a city museum.

segments.text: So where does the idea of a pagan Krampus come from? In the nineteenth century, writers such as Jacob Grimm looked for traces of a pre-Christian past in later customs. Grimm wrote that he could well imagine that even in heathen times, a god whose coming heralded a happy time had a merry elf or dwarf at his side. He was imagining, not quoting a record. Masked winter processions, like the Perchten runs held around early January, seemed to fit such ideas. And in some places, these customs had already mixed with the Nicholas custom by the eighteenth century.
